source: Stechly, Marquez, Kambhampati (2023) GPT-4 Doesn't Know It's Wrong
finding: GPT-4 as verifier of graph colorings almost never accepted a candidate: it under-accepts, the reverse of human over-acceptance.
numbers: 500 colorings, 118 correct: GPT-4 called only 30 correct, and was right 5 times. Of 100 optimal colorings it accepted 2. In self-critique runs a correct coloring appeared in 40 of 100 instances during back-prompting; the verifier missed it in all 40 (39 hallucinated a bad edge). Only 4 of 100 runs were stopped by the LLM verifier, none correct.
limits: Graph coloring only, GPT-4 (2023), one prompt style.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: same-model checking failed by rejecting right answers. Measure false-reject as well as false-accept.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) On the Self-Verification Limitations of LLMs on Reasoning and Planning Tasks
finding: Self-critique collapses; a sound external verifier gives large gains, and plain re-sampling with the sound verifier keeps most of the gain.
numbers: Success rates: Game of 24 standard 5%, LLM+LLM 3%, LLM+sound verifier 36-38%, sampling k=25 42%; Graph Coloring 16% / 2% / 34-38% / 44%; Blocksworld 40% / 55% / 60-87% / 72%; Mystery Blocksworld 4% / 0% / 6-10% / 14%. LLM verifier Table 2: Game24 FPR 10.4%, FNR 20.7%; Blocksworld FPR 6.5%, FNR 15.5%; Mystery BW FPR 18.55%; coloring FNR 95.8%.
limits: GPT-4 only; domains with exact checkers; 15-round timeout.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 2. Where a program can check exactly, the veto beats the model verdict. Generating more and letting the program pick beats critique.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR)
finding: Without an oracle label, intrinsic self-correction does not help and often hurts; oracle-label gains are an artifact.
numbers: GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 -> 74.7 (5 calls); CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 (round 1) then 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 -> 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 -> 89.0; CSQA 82.0 -> 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 -> 43.0. With oracle labels GPT-4 GSM8K 97.5, HotpotQA 59.0.
limits: Prompted self-correction in 2023 models; two rounds; no external tools.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 4, 10. Extra self-check on a single model lowered accuracy on QA. Test any check step against one-pass baseline at equal tokens.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A critical survey
finding: Survey of self-correction: no prior work shows success with feedback from prompted LLMs in general tasks; it works with reliable external feedback or large-scale fine-tuning.
numbers: Coverage to May 2024. Findings: (1) no success with prompted-LLM feedback outside tasks exceptionally suited; (2) works where reliable external feedback exists; (3) fine-tuning enables it; (4) bottleneck is feedback generation.
limits: Literature review; later reasoning models not covered.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 2. Supports giving the program (tests, solver) the veto and the model the generation.

source: Panickssery, Bowman, Feng (2024) LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
finding: LLM judges recognise their own text and score it higher; self-preference correlates linearly with self-recognition.
numbers: GPT-4 73.5% accurate at picking itself out from two other LLMs and humans; GPT-3.5 and Llama 2 over 90% self-recognition after fine-tuning on 500 examples. Summaries (CNN/DM, XSUM). Self-recognition vs self-preference Kendall tau 0.41 before fine-tuning.
limits: Summary quality judging, not correctness checking.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 10. A same-family checker likely favours its own candidate; supports a different-family or independent checker.

source: Wataoka, Takahashi, Ri (2024) Self-Preference Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge
finding: GPT-4 shows significant self-preference across eight LLMs; the bias tracks low perplexity (familiar text), not authorship.
numbers: Eight LLMs measured with a fairness-style metric; GPT-4 largest bias. LLMs give higher scores to low-perplexity outputs more than human raters do, including text they did not write.
limits: Pairwise dialogue evaluation; human labels as reference.
agent_relevance: Gap 1. Same-family checkers over-accept familiar-looking answers; use program checks or another family.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
finding: Strong LLM judges agree with humans over 80%, but show position, verbosity and self-enhancement bias and limited reasoning grading.
numbers: Over 80% agreement with controlled and crowd human preferences, same as human-human agreement.
limits: Open-ended chat preference, not correctness of reasoning; only the abstract was read.
agent_relevance: Gap 1. Judges are usable for preference but have named biases to control.

source: Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate -- Rethink Evaluation and Embrace Model Heterogeneity (2025)
finding: Five debate methods over nine benchmarks and four models rarely beat chain-of-thought or self-consistency, even with far more compute; mixing two model families helps.
numbers: Debate methods beat CoT in about 15% of comparisons; MMLU with Claude-3.5-haiku best method +0.85%, all others at least -3.60% below CoT. Heter-SoM +6.4% over SoM-average, Heter-EoT +8.2% over EoT-average; vs CoT-average up to +5.8%; MATH gains +29 to +33 points but MBPP -2 to -10% for some methods.
limits: Gain measured against the average of two single models, not the best one; compute not matched in the heterogeneity test.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 5. Different families help in debate; single-agent baselines are strong. Partial answer: no equal-token checker test.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Are More LM Calls All You Need? Scaling Properties of Compound AI Systems
finding: Majority voting and filter-vote accuracy first rises then falls with the number of calls, because easy queries improve and hard queries worsen.
numbers: Theory plus experiments: more calls raise accuracy on easy queries and lower it on hard ones; the optimum call count can be predicted from a small sample.
limits: Vote and Filter-Vote only, not program-loop scaffolds.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4, 8. Easy-gain, hard-loss within one model matches the Dell'Acqua frontier pattern; check scaffold gain by difficulty tier.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Coverage rises log-linearly with samples; with an automatic verifier it becomes accuracy; majority vote and reward models plateau near 100 samples.
numbers: MATH with Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000; majority vote or reward model only 40.50% to 41.41%.
limits: Math and code; reward model ArmoRM-Llama3-8B.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2, 6. A program-side exact verifier turns sampling into gain; model-side selection does not.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: Top LLMs drop on average 39% from single-turn to multi-turn underspecified tasks, mostly from unreliability; they lock onto early assumptions and prior attempts.
numbers: Six generation tasks, 200,000+ simulated conversations; average drop 39%; aptitude -15%, unreliability +112%. o3 and DeepSeek-R1 degrade similarly. Recap and snowball help some but stay below single-turn; recap is unrealistic since the last turn is unknown.
agent_relevance: Gap 7. Closest controlled analogue of state lost after hand-back: prior own attempts are over-relied on. Pass a clean state summary.

source: Lenat et al. (2025) A Novel Skill Modeling Approach (reproduces the Hollnagel 1993 COCOM table, p.22)
finding: Secondary but exact reproduction of the COCOM table: modes defined by number of goals, subjectively available time, choice of next action and evaluation of outcome.
numbers: Strategic: several goals, abundant time, prediction-based, elaborate evaluation. Tactical attended: several limited goals, limited but adequate time, plan based, normal. Tactical unattended: more than adequate time, unreflective, imprecise. Opportunistic: one or two competing goals, short or inadequate time, association based, cursory. Scrambled: one goal, very limited time, random, rudimentary. Mode choice depends on perceived time and familiarity.
agent_relevance: Gap 3. Mode names map to budget: abundant tokens -> plan and predict, scarce -> quick association answer. Testable as a budget rule.

source: Stanton, Ashleigh, Roberts, Xu (2001) Testing Hollnagel's contextual control model: assessing team behaviour in a human supervisory control task
finding: Reported as the first independent test of COCOM: teams in a simulated energy distribution task could be reliably coded into the four modes, and moves between modes followed the predicted linear progression.
numbers: Only abstract-level statements seen in search results; sample size and coding agreement not read (postprint server returned 503).
limits: Team-level, simulated supervisory task, one study; no LLM test.
agent_relevance: Gap 3. COCOM has thin independent human support; no LLM budget test found.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems -- recheck against later work
finding: No replication of the 45% single-agent threshold was found outside the original six benchmarks; 2502.08788 and 2403.02419 are indirect support that more agents or calls often fail to beat a strong single baseline.
numbers: No new numbers. Indirect: debate beat CoT in about 15% of comparisons (2502.08788).
limits: Absence of evidence after a limited search (Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex queries returned errors).
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open for program-loop scaffolds.

source: Gap 6 note: token cost of verification not reported in Stechly 2024 or Brown 2024
finding: No opened source reports tokens per solved item for a verify loop against a plain arm; only sample counts and round caps.
numbers: Stechly 2024: up to 15 rounds, sampling k=15 or 25; Brown 2024: up to 10,000 samples.
limits: Cost per solved item must be measured in our own harness.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open; run an equal-token comparison.

source: Gap 10 note: no direct felt-versus-measured study of an LLM judging its own scaffolded output
finding: Closest evidence: self-correction lowered accuracy, and self-recognition drives self-preference. No scaffold-specific study found.
numbers: Huang: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 after one self-correction round. Panickssery: self-preference tau 0.41 with self-recognition before tuning.
limits: Inference by juxtaposition, not a direct test.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open; score only with program checks.
